lesson.title: Randomized Block Design: Grouping First, Then Randomizing
lesson.summary: A randomized block design sorts subjects into blocks that share a known trait likely to affect the outcome, then randomly assigns treatments separately within each block, reducing the effect of that trait on the comparison.
lesson.body:
Plain random assignment, discussed in the previous section, spreads every trait roughly evenly across treatment groups given a large enough sample. But when researchers already know that a particular trait strongly affects the outcome, they do not have to leave its balancing entirely to chance. A randomized block design first sorts subjects into blocks, groups that share a similar value on that known trait, and only then randomly assigns treatments separately within each block. This borrows the logic of a stratified random sample, where a population is divided into strata before sampling from each one, and applies it to experiments instead of surveys.

The known trait used to form blocks is often called a nuisance variable, a source of variability that is not the thing being studied but that could otherwise obscure the treatment's real effect if left unbalanced. Blocking removes the variation between blocks from the comparison entirely, since every block contains its own separately randomized mini-experiment, one comparing treatments only among subjects who are already alike on that trait. What is left over, the variation within each block, is smaller and easier to attribute to the treatment, which generally makes true treatment effects easier to detect.

Consider a hypothetical fertilizer experiment. A researcher wants to compare a new fertilizer to the standard one across 80 tomato plants, but the plants are grown in two different fields, one with sandy soil and one with clay soil, and soil type is known to strongly affect plant growth regardless of fertilizer. Rather than randomizing fertilizer assignment across all 80 plants at once, the researcher blocks by field: within the 40 sandy-soil plants, 20 are randomly assigned to the new fertilizer and 20 to the standard; within the 40 clay-soil plants, the same random 20-and-20 split happens independently. Soil type can no longer masquerade as a fertilizer effect, because both fertilizers are compared on equal footing within each soil type.

It matters that random assignment still happens inside each block; blocking without randomization within blocks is not a randomized block design at all, just an uncontrolled grouping. The randomization inside each block is what protects against the unknown confounders described earlier, sun exposure, watering variation, individual plant vigor, while the blocking itself handles the one confounder the researcher already knows about and wants to neutralize directly rather than leave to chance.

Blocking is worth the extra structure only when the blocking variable genuinely affects the outcome; blocking on a trait that has little relationship to the response mostly adds complexity without much statistical payoff. When researchers can identify a variable, soil type, gender, age group, baseline severity, that plausibly matters and is measurable before the experiment begins, a randomized block design typically produces a more sensitive comparison than fully random assignment across the whole group. Matched pairs design, covered next, is simply this same idea taken to its smallest possible block size, two.
